title: Explain why a promising choice is best
chapter: Prove a limit, then build an example
goal: Explain why balanced parts give the largest product, and handle restrictions.

scenes.visual: A loop of string of fixed length forms a long thin rectangle, then morphs steadily into a square. An area counter rises as it becomes more balanced.
scenes.narration: Take a fixed length of fence and make a rectangle. A long thin rectangle encloses very little. As the sides become more equal, the area grows. Balanced parts give bigger products.

scenes.visual: A list of trial rectangles with a tick on the largest and a question "why?".
scenes.narration: You could discover this by trying examples. But in a competition you need to know it is always true, and what to do when perfect balance is not allowed.

scenes.visual: Text: "Two whole numbers add to 12." A row of pairs waits. Question: "What is the largest possible product?"
scenes.narration: Two positive whole numbers add to twelve. What is the largest their product can be? Pause and try a few pairs.

scenes.visual: Pairs with products: 1 and 11 give 11; 2 and 10 give 20; 3 and 9 give 27; 4 and 8 give 32; 5 and 7 give 35; 6 and 6 give 36. A bar chart rises to the middle.
scenes.narration: One and eleven give eleven. Two and ten give twenty. Three and nine, twenty-seven. Four and eight, thirty-two. Five and seven, thirty-five. Six and six give thirty-six. The product climbs as the numbers get closer.

scenes.visual: A 6 by 6 square. A strip of width d is cut from one side and attached to the other, forming a (6 - d) by (6 + d) rectangle with a small d by d corner square left over, shaded.
scenes.narration: Here is why. Write the two numbers as six minus d and six plus d. Start with a six by six square. Move a strip from one side to the other. The pieces no longer fit: a small square of side d is missing. So the product is thirty-six minus d squared. The further from balance, the more you lose.

scenes.visual: Rule added: "the two numbers must be different". The 6 and 6 pair greys out; 5 and 7 glows with 35.
scenes.narration: Now add a restriction: the two numbers must be different. Six and six is no longer allowed. Choose the most balanced pair that is allowed, five and seven, giving thirty-five.

scenes.visual: 12 split into three parts 4, 4, 4 with product 64, compared with 6, 6 at 36 and 3, 3, 3, 3 at 81.
scenes.narration: The same idea works with more parts. Splitting twelve into four, four and four gives sixty-four. Splitting into four threes gives eighty-one, which is the best of all for twelve. Equal parts win, and threes are especially good.

scenes.visual: Lines: "Fixed sum: balance for the biggest product", "If balance is forbidden, get as close as allowed".
scenes.narration: With a fixed total, balanced parts give the largest product. When a rule forbids perfect balance, get as close as the rule allows. Notebook challenge: a rectangle with whole-number sides has perimeter twenty-two. What is its largest possible area?

notebook_exercise: A rectangle with whole-number sides has perimeter 22. Largest possible area?
notebook_answer: Sides add to 11; 5 and 6 give area 30.
